tip: Many comparatives change their last stem sound: короткий becomes короче (korotkiy to koroche = shorter), the к turning into ч.
уже (uzhe = narrower) looks exactly like уже meaning already; stress and context tell the two apart.
лучше (luchshe = better) is the irregular comparative of хороший (khoroshiy = good), not a regular ending you can predict.
A possessive matches the noun, not you: книга (kniga = book) is feminine, so my is моя (moya), not мой (moy).
место (mesto = seat) is neuter, so your becomes твоё (tvoyo); masculine would be твой (tvoy), feminine твоя (tvoya).
Её (yeyo = her), его (yego = his), их (ikh = their) never change form, unlike мой (moy) or наш (nash): Её платье (platye = dress) keeps Её.
The ending -ся/-сь means it happened on its own: машина (mashina = car) сломалась (slomalas = broke down), nobody broke it.
готов (gotov = ready) is a short adjective for a state, and Russian adds no word for is: заказ готов (zakaz gotov = order ready).
After a comparative you can drop than and put the noun in genitive: теплее весны (teplee vesny = warmer than spring), весна (vesna) becoming весны.
Use свой (svoy) when the owner is the subject: Я взял свою книгу (ya vzyal svoyu knigu = I took my own book), not мою (moyu).
свой (svoy) means his own here because he is the subject; using его (yego) would hint the passport belongs to someone else.
With нравится (nravitsya = likes), the person goes in dative: Моему другу (moyemu drugu), and музыка (muzyka) is the grammatical subject.
самый (samyy = most) before an adjective builds the superlative and agrees in gender: самый умный ученик (samyy umnyy uchenik = smartest student).
Use чем (chem = than) to compare against an adverb: счастливее (schastlivee = happier), чем раньше (ranshe = before).
Russian says have with у (u) plus genitive: У моего брата есть собака (u moyego brata yest sobaka = my brother has a dog).
Вместо (vmesto = instead of) takes the genitive: Вместо чая (vmesto chaya), чай (chay) becoming чая.
То ли... то ли (to li... to li) means either... or with a note of uncertainty: То ли дождь (dozhd = rain), то ли снег (sneg = snow).
The preposition sits before который (kotoryy = which): на котором мы ехали (na kotorom my yekhali = on which we rode), not который alone up front.
Чей (chey = whose) agrees with the thing owned: Чей ребёнок (rebyonok = child) is masculine; use чья (chya) for feminine, чьё (chyo) for neuter.
A comparative plus всех (vsekh = of all) makes a superlative: вкуснее всех (vkusnee vsekh = tastier than all), meaning the tastiest.
худший (khudshiy = worst) is the one-word superlative of плохой (plokhoy = bad); лучший (luchshiy) is its opposite, best.
такой же... как (takoy zhe... kak) means as... as, showing equality: такая же умная, как мама (takaya zhe umnaya, kak mama = as smart as mom).
Чем... тем (chem... tem) means the more X, the more Y: Чем раньше встанешь, тем больше успеешь (chem ranshe vstanesh, tem bolshe uspeesh).
